c1-53.title: Launching a new brand
c1-53.story: Anna was spending the summer as an intern at a small Kyiv startup that was about to launch a line of reusable water bottles. The team had already chosen a packaging [[vendor]] in Lviv, and the [[branding]] was nearly finished: bright colors, a short name, and a friendly logo. The real debate was about [[pricing]]. Max, who had joined as a designer, argued that the bottle should be cheap enough for the [[mass market]], not just for serious athletes. Anna pulled up the survey results, and almost every [[respondent]] said they would happily pay a little more for a bottle that kept drinks cold all day. In a lab test, their bottle had beaten the industry [[benchmark]] by three full hours. Anna argued that this was their strongest [[use case]]: long train rides, hot summers, and school days. Her manager agreed, and they shifted the [[targeting]] of their online ads toward commuters and students. When the first hundred orders arrived that evening, Max grinned and called the cold bottle a small [[game changer]].

c1-54.title: A deal between companies
c1-54.story: Anna's dad had spent months negotiating a [[joint venture]] between his small [[pharma]] company and a lab in Poland. The Polish side held a [[patent]] for a cheaper way to produce a common allergy medicine. On Friday, both teams finally signed a [[memorandum]] of understanding at the regional health [[directorate]]. At dinner, Grandpa, who had run a dairy [[cooperative]] for twenty years, wanted to know who would actually pay for the new factory. Dad explained that a [[consortium]] of three banks would finance it, and a local [[developer]] would build it on an empty site near the river. Grandpa then asked whether anyone at those banks had a [[business interest]] in Dad's competitors. Dad laughed and admitted that the lawyers had spent a whole week checking exactly that. Satisfied, Grandpa raised his cup of tea and wished the new [[venture]] good luck.

c1-55.title: Trade at the port
c1-55.story: On a class trip to the port in Odesa, Anna and Max followed a guide past rows of colorful shipping containers. She pointed to a huge grain ship and explained that it was pumping out the seawater it had carried as [[ballast]] on the empty journey in. She added that Ukraine is a major [[exporter]] of wheat and that each terminal has a strict monthly [[quota]] to meet. Inside a warehouse, sacks of grain rolled along a noisy [[conveyor]] toward the loading dock. Next door, a coffee [[importer]] was unloading beans from Brazil, and Max immediately asked if he could get a free sample. The guide laughed and told them about a nineteenth-century [[industrialist]] who had built half of the old warehouses. Back then, some merchants still relied on [[barter]], trading grain for cloth or tools instead of money. She also described how an [[embargo]] in another region had once left ships waiting in the harbor for weeks. While the class waited for their bus by the old tram [[depot]], Max proudly showed everyone the [[tax-free]] chocolate from the ferry terminal.

c1-56.title: Money around the world
c1-56.story: Sofia, Max's sister, keeps a tin of foreign coins and bills that relatives and friends have brought her from their travels. One rainy afternoon, she spread them all over the kitchen table and asked Anna to help sort them by country. The heaviest coin was a Swiss [[franc]], which Grandpa had given her after a business trip to Geneva. Next to it lay a crisp ten-[[yuan]] note from Lisa's trip to Shanghai and a worn Turkish [[lira]] from a holiday in Istanbul. Ira had once sent her a Kenyan [[shilling]] with a wild animal on it, which instantly became the favorite of Anna's little brother, Taras. Anna found a Danish [[krone]] with a small hole in the middle, and nobody could explain why it had one. The mystery coin turned out to be a Jordanian [[dinar]], although Sofia had no idea who had brought it. Finally, Anna picked up a British pound and reminded everyone that the official name of the currency is pound [[sterling]]. Sofia decided to label each coin and turn the collection into a little map of the world for her bedroom wall.

c1-57.title: Inside an investment bank
c1-57.story: For a university project, Anna spent a day shadowing Lisa's aunt, who works in [[asset management]] at a large bank in Kyiv. In the morning, they met a former trader who now ran a small [[hedge fund]] and talked very fast about markets in Asia. Later, a colleague from [[risk management]] explained that her job was to imagine everything that could go wrong and plan for it. Anna asked how ordinary people could invest, and Lisa's aunt showed her how to open an account at an online [[brokerage]]. She also explained that some companies share their profits with investors by paying a [[dividend]] every quarter. Over lunch, the conversation turned serious when someone mentioned a recent scandal involving an [[insider]] who had leaked confidential plans to reporters before a merger. Lisa's aunt said that trust was the most valuable thing a bank had, and that it could be lost in a single day. On the way home, Anna decided that her project would focus on honesty in finance rather than on quick profits.

c1-58.title: A company in trouble
c1-58.story: Ira's mother runs a small furniture workshop outside Kyiv, and this autumn it nearly went under. A big client had delayed payment for months, which created a serious [[cash flow]] problem. Soon her largest [[creditor]], a timber supplier, warned that the business was heading toward [[default]] on its loan. An independent [[auditor]] went through every account and confirmed that the company was healthy apart from that one unpaid invoice. With his report in hand, Ira's mother asked the bank for a [[grace period]] of sixty days. The bank agreed, and a temporary [[shutdown]] of the workshop was avoided at the last minute. When the client finally paid in December, Ira helped her mother bake a cake to celebrate with all twelve employees.

c1-59.title: Planning a smart city
c1-59.story: Anna's university group was invited to a public meeting about turning an old factory district into a [[smart city]] neighborhood. The meeting took place at the local [[community center]], and the room was packed. An architect presented plans full of sensors, bike lanes, and electric buses, and Anna, who studies [[urban design]], took careful notes. Not everyone was impressed. A representative of the [[trade union]] at the old factory asked what would happen to the workers who still had jobs there. A woman from a group that does [[advocacy]] for people with disabilities pointed out that none of the new apps had been tested by blind users. Someone else mentioned the [[squatters|squatter]] who had been living in an abandoned warehouse and asked where they would go. A few older residents simply wanted to keep the [[status quo]] and insisted that the district was fine as it was. Max whispered that this kind of local [[activism]] was exactly what would make the plan better. By the end of the evening, the architect promised a second meeting and a new draft that included everyone's concerns.

c1-60.title: Generations and ideas
c1-60.story: At Sunday dinner, Anna told her family about a class debate on whether her generation could really slow down climate change. Grandpa, a proud [[boomer]] born in 1956, said he had grown up during the postwar [[baby boom]], surrounded by big plans for the future. Back then, he added, every newspaper repeated the same [[narrative]] about a perfect society just around the corner. That was why he now treated any talk of a green [[utopia]] with a healthy dose of [[skepticism]]. Anna replied that she was not naive, but that a little [[idealism]] was the only reason anyone ever tried anything new. Taras, who had just learned a new word, called Grandpa a [[cynic]], and everyone laughed. Grandpa protested that doubting something is very different from believing in nothing, and that he was simply a [[skeptic]]. Then Dad reminded him that he had put solar panels on the dacha last spring and teasingly called him a bit of a [[hypocrite]]. Grandpa smiled, said the panels were only there to save money, and passed Anna the potatoes.
